extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers and worldbuilders designing magic systems (fantasy and science fiction)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating and using magic systems in fictional worldbuilding, covering principles for how magic should be defined, limited, and revealed to serve story conflict and tone. Applicable to fantasy and science-fiction authors deciding whether and how to include magic in a setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanderson's First Law: reader understanding vs solving conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: “An author’s ability to solve conflict with magic is directly proportional to how well the reader understands said magic.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not give characters abilities unless the story has already shown they possess them. Before changing the magic system, determine how problems can be solved without magic or within the existing system. Avoid granting new abilities that perfectly solve a problem (deus ex machina); breaking this law makes magic too convenient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanderson's Second Law: limitations are greater than powers
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize what characters cannot do (limits, costs, restrictions, weaknesses). Well-defined limits force characters to struggle, push the story into interesting directions, and add dimension, depth, and tension. Gains from limits often outweigh gains from extra powers that resolve everything.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanderson's Third Law: expand what you have before adding new
rubrics_metrics.description: “Expand what you already have before you add something new.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer refining and extending existing elements of the magic system instead of introducing brand-new mechanics. Adding new elements can make the system unnecessarily complicated and risks internal contradictions, especially if goals could be achieved by expanding current capabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soft magic: preserve mystery and sense of wonder
rubrics_metrics.description: Soft magic is not rigidly defined (if defined at all), allowing authors to “preserve the sense of wonder in their books.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use vagueness to create amazement and tension because the reader (and characters) do not understand what is possible. Soft systems tend to be dangerous, unpredictable, and should not be used to conveniently solve plot problems; characters remain small relative to vast unknown powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hard magic: explicit rules and predictable limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Hard magic is where “the author explicitly describes the rules of magic.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define clearly what magic can and cannot do so readers are not surprised when characters use abilities. Maintain consistency (no spur-of-the-moment new powers). A well-defined rule-set lets readers accept characters using the tools already provided; examples include comic-book style abilities like Spider-Man's power set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Middle-ground systems: mix definition with mystery
rubrics_metrics.description: A hybrid approach where some aspects of magic are defined and others remain mysterious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine the benefits of hard and soft magic: provide enough structure for readers to understand and follow the story while leaving some aspects unexplained to preserve wonder and flexibility. Use this to balance predictability and mystery without overcomplicating the system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary consideration: decide whether and why your world needs magic
rubrics_metrics.description: Before inventing spells or systems of magic, consider whether your world needs or should have magic and understand your options and theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worldbuilders should first determine the role of magic in the setting (e.g., whether SF settings will use technology vs magic) and then choose a system type (hard/soft/mixed) and guiding principles accordingly. This upstream decision shapes the rules, narrative uses, and tone of the magic throughout the story.
